question: What are the basic ideas of supervised learning (regression and classification), and how do least squares and nearest neighbours illustrate the tradeoffs between bias, variance, model assumptions and dimension?

limits: Simulations are low-dimensional or contrived; the authors call the exp(-8||X||^2) example 'highly contrived'.
Chapter gives no numeric error rates in text for Figs 2.4, 2.7 and 2.9; those only appear as plotted curves.
Test-error estimation is deferred to Chapter 7; the chapter itself offers no practical method to choose k or lambda.
The additive error model Y=f(X)+eps is stated as an approximation and is not used for qualitative outputs.
Dates from 2009: no coverage of deep nets beyond single-layer networks, nor of modern double descent behaviour (Fig 2.11 shows the classical U-shaped test curve).
practices: Do not pick complexity (k, lambda, number of basis functions) by training error, since it would always choose the interpolating fit (Sec 2.9, Sec 2.3.2).
Compare methods on an independent test set rather than training misclassification (Sec 2.3.2).
Code a K-level categorical output with K dummy variables, only one on at a time (Sec 2.2).
For a two-class problem, regress a 0/1 target and classify to ORANGE if fitted value exceeds 0.5 (Sec 2.2, Eq 2.7).
Use squared-error loss for regression, L1 when robustness to outliers is wanted, and 0-1 loss for classification (Sec 2.4).
In high dimensions, impose structure (additivity, linearity, adaptive metrics) rather than rely on local averaging (Sec 2.5-2.7).
Restrict the class of fitted functions with a penalty, kernel or basis expansion, because unrestricted RSS minimisation has infinitely many interpolating solutions (Sec 2.7-2.8).

terms.definition: use of inputs, measured or preset, to predict the values of one or more outputs
regression when we predict quantitative outputs, and classification when we predict qualitative outputs
a K-level qualitative variable is represented by a vector of K binary variables or bits, only one of which is on at a time
a set of measurements (x_i, y_i) or (x_i, g_i), i=1..N, with which to construct the prediction rule
sum over i of (y_i - x_i^T beta)^2; minimised by beta_hat = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y when X^T X is nonsingular
Y_hat(x) = (1/k) sum of y_i over x_i in N_k(x), the k training points closest to x
E(Y - f(X))^2 under squared error loss; also known as test or generalization error
f(x) = E(Y | X = x), the conditional expectation
classify to the most probable class using Pr(G|X); its error rate is called the Bayes rate
breakdown of local methods in high dimensions, since neighbourhoods needed to capture a fixed fraction of data stop being local (Bellman, 1961)
sigma^2, the variance of the new test target, beyond our control even if f is known
PRSS(f; lambda) = RSS(f) + lambda J(f); J is large for functions that vary too rapidly; corresponds to a log-prior, so minimising gives the posterior mode
f_hat(x0) = sum K_lambda(x0,x_i) y_i / sum K_lambda(x0,x_i), a kernel-weighted average
adaptively chosen basis function methods where one has available a possibly infinite set D of candidate basis functions and builds models by some search mechanism
